text: She is yellow and she is small. Someone has painted 007 on the door and the bullet holes are fake, but nobody laughs. People walk around her like an old horse.
There used to be a factory here. Quai de Javel, the chimneys, the noise of the presses from morning to night. Workers went in by the thousand and steel came out as cars.
Today there is grass and clipped hedges. People stroll where others worked. The 2CV doesn't know. She waits, leaning a little, like a car that remembers.
2cv-007.note: In 1929 the Citroën works on the Quai de Javel employed thousands of workers. They closed in 1975; the Parc André-Citroën opened on the site in 1992.

art.commons: Usines Citroën, quai de Javel - btv1b532138417.jpg
art.caption: Agence Rol, Citroën works, Quai de Javel, 1929

2cv-007.when: Quai de Javel · 1929, the factory gates
scene: The siren howls and the gates open. We pour out in our thousands, in blue overalls, hands black, ears still ringing from the presses. The quay smells of oil, of hot iron and of the river.

Behind us the assembly line keeps going without us; the night shift is already in. A car every few minutes, they say, more than anywhere in Europe. Monsieur Citroën has put his name in lights on the Eiffel Tower. Down here, his name is on our pay slips, and they are thin.

I light a cigarette and walk along the Seine with the others. Someone is talking about a strike, someone else about a girl, someone about the football. The chimneys smoke against the pink sky. Tomorrow at six, the siren again. For now, the evening belongs to us.
2cv-007.approach: I head back down towards the Seine by rue de la Montagne-d'Aulas. The sky opens, the buildings draw apart. Where the Citroën assembly lines once ran there is a park. I go there to finish the spiral.

text: The stone is white and the faces are grave. A woman holds a child. A soldier looks far off, towards something we cannot see.
It is a fine day. The leaves are still green above the railings. A man walks by with his bread and doesn't look up. The names have been there for a hundred years; they're used to it.
In July 1919 Paris marched under the Arc de Triomphe. Then towns and neighbourhoods carved their dead in stone, so that the numbers would keep their names.
monument-aux-morts-15e.note: On 14 July 1919 the Victory Parade crossed Paris behind Marshals Joffre and Foch. War memorials then went up all over France.

art.commons: Maréchal Ferdinand Foch saluant du bâton, à cheval, 14 juillet 1919.jpg
art.caption: Marshal Foch at the Victory Parade, 14 July 1919

scene: We have been standing since the night to get a place. People have climbed into the trees, onto the lamp posts, onto the roofs of the kiosks. A boy sells periscopes made of cardboard and mirrors. My mother holds my hand so hard it hurts.

First come the wounded. Men without legs in little carts, men without faces behind white masks. The crowd stops cheering. Nobody knows what to do with their hands. Then the marshals on horseback, Joffre, Foch, and the noise comes back like a wave, enormous, shaking the windows.

My father is not in the parade. He is in a field near Verdun, under a white cross with a number. My mother waves her handkerchief at the soldiers who are passing anyway. She is smiling. Tears run down her face. I do not understand yet that both can be true at once.
monument-aux-morts-15e.approach: Place Henri-Queuille, then rue Péclet. The 15th is Paris on a weekday: schools, bakeries, a town hall with tired flags. In front of it, a soldier made of stone.

text: The bronze medallion has turned green, and the stone has streaked beneath it like a tear that took its time. It is Stendhal. He looks like a man who has dined well and won't tell you about it.
Leaves fall on the lawn. Students go by without looking. He would have looked. He looked at everything: women, uniforms, ambition on faces.
In 1830 he published The Red and the Black. Paris was young, poor and sure of itself. The garden was already here. It still is.
stendhal-rodin.note: Henri Beyle, known as Stendhal (1783–1842), portrayed in 1840. The Red and the Black appeared in 1830, the year of the July Revolution.

art.commons: Portrait de Stendhal en 1840, 88.23.jpg
art.caption: Portrait of Stendhal in 1840

scene: I walk the paths with my manuscript under my arm. The gravel crunches. Students in frock coats argue about Hugo under the chestnut trees, and a nursemaid pretends not to listen while she listens to everything.

I sit on a bench and watch them. Ambition is written on their faces like a rash. They have read about Napoleon; they want to be him by Thursday. I know the look. I wore it at their age, in a uniform that was too big for me.

The hero of my book will be called Julien. He will be poor, handsome and impatient, and he will lose everything for having wanted too much. I write a line on my knee, cross it out, write it again. The fountain splashes. Paris is young, broke and sure of itself, and so am I, a little.
stendhal-rodin.approach: Rue de Tournon, the gentle slope towards the Senate. The gilded gates of the Luxembourg. Inside, the gravel crunches and the green chairs wait for someone. I look for a face in bronze under the chestnut trees.

text: In the window a Black man in a general's uniform looks back at us. Sabre at his side, chin raised. The book is called The Black Devil.

It is Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, father of the novelist. Son of an enslaved woman from Saint-Domingue, he became commander-in-chief of the armies of the Republic. The Austrians, they say, called him the black devil.
He had almost been forgotten. Then a book, a window, a passer-by who stops. That is how the dead come back: through the street.
le-diable-noir.note: Commander-in-chief from 1793, Thomas-Alexandre Dumas (1762–1806) was the first general of Afro-Caribbean origin in the French army.

art.commons: Thomas-Alexandre Dumas.jpg
art.caption: General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas

scene: It is snowing on the pass and the men are hungry. The general walks in front, on foot, with us. He is taller than any of us by a head, and when he laughs you can hear it over the wind. His father was a marquis, his mother a slave in Saint-Domingue. Here, nobody cares. Here, he is the one who goes first.

The Austrians hold the redoubts above us. We climb at night, with crampons on our boots, rope in our hands. My fingers no longer feel the rope. Beside me a drummer boy is praying in Breton. Up ahead, the general's silhouette stops, turns, signals: now.

We take the redoubts at dawn. The prisoners look at him with their mouths open; they call him der schwarze Teufel, the black devil. He gives them his own bread. Later, in Paris, they will forget his name for two hundred years. I will not.
le-diable-noir.approach: Pont Neuf. Henri IV on his horse, barges sliding beneath, water slapping the piers. On the Left Bank, the bookshops of Odéon turn their windows towards me like faces.

text: The paper is folded in one hand. On the front page, an enormous mosquito and the word enemy. Lower down, the heatwave, record temperatures.
Paris has always read its fears in the morning. Yesterday it was the Apaches, crimes from the outskirts in garish colours. Today an insect and the rising heat.
The hand holds the paper the way you hold a ticket. It will be read on the métro. Then left on a seat for someone else.
le-parisien.note: Around 1900 the illustrated supplements of Le Petit Journal printed crime stories and the fear of the 'Apaches' in full colour.

art.commons: Le Petit Journal - Apache.jpg
art.caption: Le Petit Journal, illustrated supplement, 'The Apache'

le-parisien.when: Paris, a morning in 1907 · at the kiosk
scene: The vendor shouts the headline before you can read it: another Apache crime! On the colour cover a man in a flat cap holds a knife over a gentleman in a top hat, and the blood is the brightest red the printers have.

Everyone buys it. The concierge, the clerk, the lady with the little dog. We read it on the platform of the tram and shiver with pleasure. The Apaches live out in Belleville, in Charonne, in the fortifications; we have never met one. That is what makes them so frightening.

By noon the paper is wrapping fish at the market. By evening it is lining a drawer. Tomorrow there will be another crime, another colour cover, another little thrill bought for five centimes. Paris eats its fear for breakfast.
le-parisien.approach: On rue du Louvre the cafés are putting out their iron chairs. A green kiosk, the morning papers stacked under a pebble. I read the headline upside down without stopping.

text: The stone says: Galerie d'Apollon. The letters are gilded and a little worn at the edges. Above, the ceiling opens onto gods and clouds.
You go in with the crowd. It is warm. The guards watch hands, not paintings. A child asks where the sun is, and someone points at the ceiling.
Hubert Robert was already painting the Grand Gallery as a covered street, full of light and people. The museum was new. It belonged to everyone. It still does, provided you queue.
louvre-galerie-apollon.note: Hubert Robert, one of the Museum's curators, imagined the Grand Gallery lit from above around 1796. The Louvre has been open to the public since 1793.

art.commons: Hubert Robert - The Grande Galerie - WGA19594.jpg
art.caption: Hubert Robert, The Grand Gallery of the Louvre, c. 1795

louvre-galerie-apollon.when: Paris, 10 August 1793 · the Museum opens its doors
scene: Yesterday it was the palace of kings. Today we walk in without paying, in clogs if we like. The guard at the door does not bow to anyone; he wears a cockade and looks at our hands, not our faces. Behind me a fishwife from Les Halles is still carrying her basket.

The Grand Gallery goes on forever. Light falls from tall windows onto canvases that only princes have seen. A man in a worn coat stops in front of a Raphael and takes his hat off, as if he were in church. His wife pulls his sleeve. He does not move.

I came for an hour. I stay until they close. When I come out the river is gold and the Republic is one year old. I have no money, no land, no name anyone will remember. But for one afternoon all of this belonged to me.
louvre-galerie-apollon.approach: I cross the Pont des Arts. The planks ring under my soles, the wind comes from the west and smells of water. Opposite, the Louvre's façade takes the sun, long as a century. I go in through the Porte des Lions.

text: The same question four times on the wall: Are you a communist? Join us. The paper is new, the glue has dripped. Someone has already started tearing them down.
The walls of Paris have always spoken loudly. You paste, you tear, you paste again. Posters last as long as the night.
In 1936 hundreds of thousands marched, fists raised, to the wall of the Fédérés. The flags were red. The summer was long. People mostly remember the paid holidays.
affiches-pcr.note: May 1936: the Popular Front procession climbs to the Communards' Wall at Père-Lachaise, where Communards were shot in 1871.

art.commons: Manifestation du Front populaire au mur des Fédérés - btv1b90282283.jpg
art.caption: Popular Front demonstration at the Communards' Wall, 1936
art.credit: Agence de presse Meurisse. Agence photographique (commanditaire)

scene: There are hundreds of thousands of us and at first we walk almost in silence. Then someone strikes up the Internationale, and it spreads up the column like fire along a fuse, until the whole of rue de la Roquette is singing.

Fists raised. Red flags, red scarves, a little girl on her father's shoulders with a red ribbon in her hair. The old men at the front walked this route as children; some of them saw the Commune. They do not sing. They cry without wiping their faces.

At the wall of the Fédérés we file past, one by one, and lay down our flowers. The stone is pocked with bullet holes. Somebody whispers that this summer we will have holidays, real paid holidays, the sea. Nobody believes it. Everybody believes it.
affiches-pcr.approach: I head down towards the Concorde by rue Saint-Florentin. The obelisk, the wind, cars going round in circles. Against a hoarding, posters pasted one on top of another, like layers of earth.

text: A red-and-white sticker on a green door. Are you a communist? Someone has crossed it out and written Rebel by hand. Revolution, says the bottom line, in capitals.
The door does not answer. It has seen worse. The word is old in Paris; it has been worn smooth in every street.
In July 1830 the city covered itself in barricades in three days. Delacroix painted a barefoot woman, a flag, the dead under her feet. The painting hangs in the Louvre. The word is on the door.
autocollant-revolution.note: Eugène Delacroix, Liberty Leading the People, 1830: the Three Glorious Days, 27, 28 and 29 July.

art.commons: Eugène Delacroix - La liberté guidant le peuple.jpg
art.caption: Eugène Delacroix, Liberty Leading the People, 1830

autocollant-revolution.when: Paris, 28 July 1830 · near the Hôtel de Ville
scene: The tocsin has been ringing since dawn. We have torn the paving stones out of the street and stacked them as high as a man, with a cart on its side and a wardrobe someone threw from a third floor. My hands are grey with dust. My mouth tastes of gunpowder and of the wine the baker poured for us at six.

Across the square the Swiss Guards hold the corner in a red line. When they fire, the noise slaps the façades and comes back twice. A boy beside me, fourteen at most, loads a pistol bigger than his forearm. He is laughing. I do not know his name. I will never know it.

By evening the tricolour is on the towers of Notre-Dame. A woman climbs the barricade with the flag in her fist, barefoot, her shawl falling, and for one second the whole street stops breathing. Then everybody shouts at once. Three days. That is all it takes to throw out a king.
autocollant-revolution.approach: I start at Point Zero, the bronze star set into the square in front of Notre-Dame. Behind me, the towers; ahead, the whole of Paris curling outward like a shell. I follow the quay, the Seine on my right. On a green door, someone has stuck a word that has already been used many times.

text: On the great blind wall, a drawing in red chalk, figures barely sketched. At the bottom someone has written Vive la Commune. The sky above is very blue.
People draw on walls what they haven't finished saying. A hundred and fifty years is nothing for a city.

In the spring of 1871, Paris governed itself for seventy-two days. There were barricades on rue de Castiglione, place Vendôme, everywhere. Then the Bloody Week, in May. Walls remember better than books.
vive-la-commune.note: March–May 1871: the Paris Commune. Photographers recorded the barricades; some of those images were later used to identify the insurgents.

art.commons: La Commune 1871. Barricade rue de Castiglione, 1er arrondissement, Paris. PH20145.jpg
art.caption: Barricade on rue de Castiglione, Paris Commune, 1871
art.credit: Attribué à Braquehais, Auguste Bruno (Dieppe, 18–01–1823 - La Celle-Saint-Cloud, 1875), photographe

scene: There is smoke everywhere. The Tuileries are burning behind us; the air smells of timber and of paper, of a whole palace of documents going up at once. Ash falls on my sleeves like grey snow. Nobody brushes it off any more.

The barricade on rue de Castiglione is taller than the ones of '48. We built it properly this time, with sandbags, with earth, with the cobbles numbered by the men from the roadworks. A woman is handing out cartridges from her apron. Her husband is somewhere near the Madeleine. She has not heard from him since Monday.

The Versaillais are coming street by street. We can hear them before we see them: the dull shots, then the silence, then the shots again, closer. Somebody writes on the wall with a lump of red chalk, slowly, so the letters will last. Vive la Commune. Then we go back to our places and wait.
vive-la-commune.approach: The quay stretches on. The booksellers open their green boxes one by one, with the patience of fishermen. A repainted wall catches my eye: red letters, a date nobody manages to erase. I slow down.

text: A white sheet pasted on a wall black with tags: It's your system that is violent, not the high-school students! Below, stencilled: NO WAR.
The handwriting is careful. Whoever pasted it took their time. Schools close at night; walls don't.
In April 1834, on rue Transnonain, soldiers entered a building and killed its residents. Daumier drew a man in a nightshirt, dead at the foot of his bed. That drawing did more than many speeches.
systeme-violent.note: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, 15 April 1834, lithograph published for L'Association mensuelle.

art.commons: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, le 15 avril 1834, 1834, NGA 6133.jpg
art.caption: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, 15 April 1834

systeme-violent.when: Paris, April 1834 · rue Transnonain, before dawn
scene: There were shots all evening. We closed the shutters and pushed the chest of drawers against the door. The child sleeps between us, his fists closed. My husband says the troops will not come up; we have done nothing, we are only weavers, we only live here.

At four the stairs shake. Boots, rifle butts, a voice shouting that someone fired from this house. Doors give way on the floor below, one after the other. A cry, then nothing. My husband stands up in his nightshirt and goes to open, his hands raised, to explain.

I do not want to tell the rest. A man with a pencil came the next week and drew the room as it was: the overturned bed, the old man on the floor, the child under his father. They say the drawing was sold in the shops for a few sous and the king had it seized. Paper remembers what soldiers forget.
systeme-violent.approach: I set off again along rue Montorgueil, then rue Rambuteau. To the east, behind the coloured pipes of the Centre Pompidou, ran the old rue Transnonain. On a metal shutter someone has sprayed the same anger.

text: Blue, black, letters climbing over each other. ZERO, huge. Then Free Gaza, Free Palestine, Mélenchon, Nik la police. The wall is a crowd talking all at once.
Nobody really listens. Everybody writes. That is how a city thinks out loud.
In 1910 the Futurists painted the crowd as a machine: bodies colliding, electric light. They believed the future would be loud. They were right.
graffitis-zero.note: Umberto Boccioni, Riot in the Galleria, 1910. The Futurists wanted to paint speed, crowds, the modern city.

art.commons: Umberto boccioni, rissa in galleria, 1910, 01.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, Riot in the Galleria, 1910

scene: The gallery is packed and everyone is talking at once. The canvases shout even louder: lines that break, horses that explode, a fight in an arcade where the bodies have turned into light. A critic next to me says it is not painting, it is noise.

The Italians are here, in black suits, very pleased with themselves. One of them climbs on a chair and starts reading a manifesto. Some people applaud, some whistle, a lady leaves with her hand over her mouth. I do not know if I love it or hate it. My heart is beating too fast to decide.

Outside, on the boulevard, an automobile honks, a tram sparks, a newspaper seller cries the evening edition. I realise they have painted exactly this: the street, the crowd, the racket. They have simply turned up the volume.
graffitis-zero.approach: I leave by rue Férou, place Saint-Sulpice and its fountain of four bishops. Rue Bonaparte, the art galleries and their white windows. Further on, a wall of slogans all shouting at the same time.

text: A black sign, white letters and a pink signature: Big Black Cook. Rue Tiquetonne. Evening falls, light spills from the windows.
The street is narrow and old. It smells of frying and stone. People eat standing up, laugh loudly, move on.
Two steps away were Les Halles. Lhermitte painted the market women, the cabbages, the baskets, the belly of Paris that never slept. The belly has moved away. The hunger stayed in the neighbourhood.
big-black-cook.note: Léon Lhermitte, Les Halles, c. 1895, Petit Palais. The market left central Paris for Rungis in 1969.

art.commons: Léon Augustin Lhermitte - Les Halles - musée des Beaux-Arts de la ville de Paris.jpg
art.caption: Léon Lhermitte, Les Halles, c. 1895

big-black-cook.when: Les Halles, four in the morning · 1895
scene: The carts came in from the country during the night. It smells of cabbage, of wet earth, of fish on ice and of horses steaming in the cold. The pavilions of iron and glass glow from inside like lanterns. Nobody here has slept.

A market woman with forearms like hams shouts the price of her leeks at me. I laugh and she laughs back and calls me her little sparrow. Porters go by with whole sides of beef on their shoulders, their white smocks stained pink. Someone is frying onions on a brazier at the corner. I have never been so hungry.

At five the bistros open their shutters. Onion soup, a glass of white wine, bread torn by hand. The coachmen, the butchers, the girls coming home from the dance halls all eat at the same zinc counter. The sky turns grey over Saint-Eustache. The belly of Paris is full.
big-black-cook.approach: Rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, rue Étienne-Marcel. The cobbles are older, the façades lean a little, as if tired. Rue Tiquetonne smells of hot oil and wet wood. I am in the belly of Paris.

text: A door open on a warm room, yellow lamps, people packed in. A woman waits outside in white trousers. A scooter sleeps in front.
You hear Italian, dishes, a radio. Paris has always eaten at other people's tables, and ended up calling it home.
Around 1880 Jean Béraud painted the boulevard des Capucines at night, in front of the Café Napolitain. Gentlemen in hats, ladies, street lamps. Naples in Paris, already.
forza-napoli.note: Jean Béraud, The Boulevard des Capucines at Night, in Front of the Café Napolitain, c. 1880.

art.commons: Béraud - Le boulevard des Capucines, le soir, devant le Café Napolitain, Vers 1880.jpg
art.caption: Jean Béraud, In Front of the Café Napolitain, c. 1880

forza-napoli.when: Paris, an evening in 1880 · boulevard des Capucines
scene: The gas lamps come on one by one; the lamplighter goes by with his pole. In front of the Café Napolitain the tables spill onto the pavement and the waiters glide between them with ices on silver trays.

A lady in a black dress sits alone, very straight, waiting for someone who is late. Two gentlemen in top hats argue about the Opéra. A flower girl offers me violets; I buy some I don't need. The air smells of horse, of coffee and of vanilla.

Inside, someone is singing in Neapolitan, a song about the sea. Nobody understands the words and everybody goes quiet. For a moment the boulevard is a quayside in the south, warm and far away. Then a carriage rattles past and we are back in Paris, happy to be.
forza-napoli.approach: I cross the Seine again. The Tuileries, then rue Saint-Honoré and its too-clean shop windows. From a half-open door comes a smell of tomato, garlic and basil. Somebody is singing in Italian in a kitchen.

text: Ink drawings pinned to a wall, handmade, 25 euros. In one, a man holds a woman up at gunpoint in a café. At the top: Kill the past, embrace the future.
A joke, perhaps. Or a manifesto. People who sell drawings never say which.
In 1910 Boccioni painted The City Rises: enormous horses, building sites, men dragged forward by the force of the new. Kill the past, they had written too. The past is still here. It sells drawings.
dessins-faits-main.note: Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910. The Futurist Manifesto appeared on the front page of Le Figaro in 1909.

art.commons: The City Rises by Umberto Boccioni 1910.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910

dessins-faits-main.when: Paris, Saturday 20 February 1909 · a newspaper kiosk
scene: I buy Le Figaro at the kiosk, as I do every Saturday. On the front page an Italian I have never heard of writes that we must burn the museums, flood the libraries, glorify war and speed. A racing car, he says, is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace.

I read it standing up, in the cold, with my gloves on. Around me Paris goes on exactly as before: an omnibus pulled by three grey horses, a girl selling violets, a gentleman with a cane. Nobody here wants to kill the past. The past is the only thing that keeps us warm.

And yet. A motor car tears down the boulevard, all brass and noise, and every head turns at once. The horses shy. Something in my chest leaps with them. I fold the paper and put it in my coat, and I do not throw it away.
dessins-faits-main.approach: I leave through the Cour Carrée and head north. The streets narrow, the façades lean closer. On a pavement, drawings clipped to a string sway in the draught.

text: A lit bus shelter. A huge, glossy dessert, ice cream inside a burger. A UFO among desserts, says the ad. Behind the glass, an ordinary street.
People wait for the bus in front of temptation. The light never goes out. The poster smiles at everyone, even those who don't look at it.
In the 1890s Jules Chéret covered Paris with colourful women selling apéritifs and balls. They said he had brought art into the street. The street mostly learned to sell.
abribus-burger-king.note: Jules Chéret (1836–1932), 'father of the modern poster'. Colour lithography turned the walls of Paris into an advertising gallery.

art.commons: Apéritif Mugnier affiche, Jules Chéret 90.jpg
art.caption: Jules Chéret, poster for Apéritif Mugnier

scene: The billposter arrives before dawn with his bucket and his brush. He unrolls the poster on the hoarding and smooths it with long strokes, from the centre out, so there are no bubbles. The paste smells of flour and glue.

When he steps back, a woman appears in the grey light: laughing, yellow and red, skirts flying, a glass raised. She is selling an apéritif. She looks happier than anyone in this street has ever been. The milkman stops his cart to look at her.

By eight o'clock the whole street has seen her. Clerks slow down, girls copy her hat, a policeman pretends not to smile. Tomorrow another poster will go over her. But today the wall is a painting, and the painting is selling something.
abribus-burger-king.approach: Place de la Madeleine, that Greek temple whose only job is to be beautiful. On the boulevard a bus shelter glows like a jewellery case, a giant burger above everyone's heads. The bus doesn't come.

text: A bank card floats on a white tiled wall. Own your money. The current account for your euros, bitcoins and stablecoins. It is the métro, somewhere under Paris.
The tiles have been the same for a hundred years. Money has become invisible. It is promised now the way electricity once was.
In 1914 Robert Delaunay painted his Homage to Blériot: discs of colour, a propeller, a plane over the Channel. The future was spinning. It still spins, smaller, in our pockets.
deblock-metro.note: Robert Delaunay, Homage to Blériot, 1914. Louis Blériot had flown across the Channel in 1909.

art.commons: Robert Delaunay, Hommage à Blériot, 1914.jpg
art.caption: Robert Delaunay, Homage to Blériot, 1914

scene: You go down under the earth and everyone falls a little silent. The white tiles throw back the electric light, so bright it hurts. It smells of fresh paint, of hot metal and of something new that has no name yet.

The train arrives without a horse, without smoke, with a long electric sigh. The doors are wooden, the seats varnished. A lady crosses herself. A boy presses his face to the window to see the tunnel go by, but there is nothing to see, only the dark and our own faces.

Porte Maillot to Vincennes in less than half an hour. Up above, the Exposition Universelle, the moving walkways, the palace of electricity. Down here, the future rattles and sways and we hold on to the brass rail. Nobody says it, but we all feel it: the city has just grown a second floor, underground.
deblock-metro.approach: I cross the gardens of Les Halles. The escalators swallow people in batches. Under my feet the city rumbles: Châtelet, a knot of tunnels and draughts. I go down a few steps, just to see.

text: The light is green. A young woman crosses, another follows, scooters wait. The façades are cream, the balconies black, the sky white.
It is the hour when everyone is going somewhere. Nobody looks at the buildings. They were built for that: to be forgotten as you walk.
In 1877 Caillebotte painted a brand-new crossroads in the rain. Umbrellas, shining cobbles, people passing without seeing one another. Traffic lights didn't exist yet. The rest is the same.
feu-vert.note: Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877, Art Institute of Chicago. The crossroads is near the Gare Saint-Lazare.

art.commons: Gustave Caillebotte - Paris Street; Rainy Day - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877

feu-vert.when: Paris, 1877 · place de Dublin, a rainy day
scene: It is raining finely, a rain that doesn't wet you, it only makes things shine. The paving stones are new, cut square, and they gleam like the backs of fish. The buildings around the crossroads are so white they look unfinished.

I hold my umbrella tilted against the wind. A couple comes towards me arm in arm, he in a grey top hat, she with a veil and a pearl at her ear. We almost collide, we step aside, we do not look at each other. That is the new city: everyone together, everyone alone.

Behind me the trains of Saint-Lazare whistle. A worker crosses with a ladder on his shoulder. The street is so wide you could lose a village in it. I stop in the middle, under my umbrella, and for a moment I am the only still point in all this movement.
feu-vert.approach: The grand boulevards give way to the Europe district, streets named after cities. A star-shaped crossroads, umbrellas, a light turning green. I cross with everyone else.

parc-de-l-etrange.place: A gate, on an October evening
text: A black tarpaulin on a gate: The Park of the Strange, the immersive Halloween event. The red letters drip on purpose. Behind, quiet trees.
Now we pay to be scared. We queue. We scream a little, laugh a lot, and come out into the ordinary night.
In 1861 Nadar went down into the catacombs with artificial light and mannequins. He photographed rows of skulls, bones stacked like wood. Beneath Paris, Halloween lasts all year.
parc-de-l-etrange.note: Félix Nadar photographed the Paris catacombs in 1861–1862, one of the first photographic series made with artificial light.

art.commons: Nadar - Catacombes de Paris - NPS 74.jpg
art.caption: Nadar, Catacombs of Paris, 1861–1862

scene: We go down a staircase that turns for a long time. The air grows cold and damp; it smells of chalk and of something older that I do not want to name. The photographer's assistant carries the batteries in a crate, swearing softly at every step.

Then the bones. Thousands of them, stacked like firewood, skulls in rows, femurs in walls. Monsieur Nadar sets up his camera and his electric lamp. The light is so white, so hard, that the shadows jump back. A skull stares at me with its two black holes. I stare back.

Each exposure lasts eighteen minutes. We stand still in the dark beside the dead, holding our breath, listening to water dripping somewhere. When we finally climb back into the daylight, rue Denfert is noisy and alive, and I have never loved the noise so much.
parc-de-l-etrange.approach: Pont de la Concorde, the esplanade of Les Invalides, the golden dome watching me go. Avenue de Breteuil, trees lined up like soldiers. I know that under my feet run the quarries: miles of neatly stacked bones.

text: A poster on scaffolding: Gospel Dream, authentic songs of the African American Church. Singers in purple robes. Église Saint-Louis-d'Antin, Friday, 8.30 pm.
You imagine the voices in the cold stone. Local people going in out of curiosity and coming out changed.
In 1925 Josephine Baker arrived from St. Louis, Missouri, and Paris lost its head. Jazz, the Charleston, the Revue Nègre. Paris often listened to Black America before America did.
gospel-dream.note: Josephine Baker photographed by Waléry around 1926. She arrived in Paris in 1925 with the Revue Nègre and became French in 1937.

art.commons: Joséphine Baker - photo Waléry.jpg
art.caption: Waléry, Josephine Baker, c. 1926

scene: I am in the balcony and it is far too hot. The ladies fan themselves with their programmes. Then the orchestra strikes up and the room falls silent all at once, as if someone had turned off the gas.

She comes on almost naked, a belt of feathers, her knees going in every direction. She crosses her eyes, she laughs, she makes fun of us. Next to me a gentleman in a dinner jacket says it is a disgrace. He doesn't take his eyes off her.
On the way out, on avenue Montaigne, I can still hear the trombone. Paris has just fallen in love with a nineteen-year-old girl from Saint Louis, Missouri. Nobody will sleep tonight. Nobody wants to.
gospel-dream.approach: Rue de Caumartin, the crowds from the department stores, paper bags bumping. At the end, almost hidden, the church of Saint-Louis-d'Antin. On the scaffolding a poster promises voices.

text: A street sign: Rue du Palais. Underneath, sprayed: Macron castration. A bicycle, the foot of a wall, pale stone.
This may not be Paris. The coat of arms looks like Grenoble's. But anger has no address.
In June 1788, in Grenoble, people climbed onto the roofs and threw tiles at the king's soldiers. It was called the Day of the Tiles. A year later came the Bastille.
rue-du-palais.note: Alexandre Debelle, The Day of the Tiles (7 June 1788), 1889, Musée de la Révolution française, Vizille.

art.commons: Journée des Tuiles (Alexandre Debelle), Musée de la Révolution française - Vizille.jpg
art.caption: Alexandre Debelle, The Day of the Tiles, 1889

rue-du-palais.when: Grenoble, 7 June 1788 · the Day of the Tiles
scene: The bells have been ringing since morning. The king wants to send our magistrates away and the town will not have it. The shops close, the market women leave their stalls, the glove-makers come out with their aprons still on.

When the soldiers advance into the square, we climb onto the roofs. I pull up the tiles with my bare hands and throw them down, one after the other, as hard as I can. They shatter on the cobbles like plates. The soldiers raise their arms over their heads. One of them looks up at me. He is my age.

By evening the magistrates are back in their palace and the whole town is singing. Nobody knows it yet, but a year from now Paris will do the same thing, louder. Revolutions do not always start in the capital.
rue-du-palais.approach: Here the shell opens and the walk leaves Paris. I take the train towards the Alps. Grenoble: mountains at the end of every street, a blue sign on the corner of a palace.

une-solution-revolution.place: Beyond the walls — a pink façade
text: A pink façade, closed shutters, a parked car. On the wall, grubby letters: One solution, revolution.
The word is written small, almost shy. Provincial walls speak more quietly than Paris walls.
On 14 July 1789 the Bastille was taken with muskets found that very morning at Les Invalides. Only seven prisoners were freed. But the word stayed, and people still write it on pink walls.
une-solution-revolution.note: Jean-Pierre Houël, The Storming of the Bastille, 1789, Bibliothèque nationale de France.

art.commons: Prise de la Bastille clean.jpg
art.caption: Jean-Pierre Houël, The Storming of the Bastille, 1789

scene: This morning at Les Invalides we took the muskets. Now we need powder, and the powder is in there, behind eight towers and walls thicker than a house. The drawbridge is up. The governor is talking. We are tired of talking.

A man climbs onto the roof of the guardhouse and cuts the chains with an axe. The bridge crashes down and a cloud of dust rises. The soldiers fire from the towers; a man falls next to me, then another. The smell of blood and powder is the same smell.

At five o'clock it is over. We find seven prisoners, a few old papers, no treasure. It doesn't matter. Somebody is already taking the stones down to sell them as souvenirs. The word is everywhere now, in every mouth: revolution.
une-solution-revolution.approach: A pink façade, somewhere else. I'm no longer sure where. The word is the same as in Paris, written bigger.

nike-la-police.place: Beyond the walls — a pink wall
text: A pink wall, a window with white shutters and, sprayed in black: Nike la police. A grey car has stopped right underneath, as if it hadn't noticed.
The word is misspelled and everyone understands it. Walls don't correct mistakes.
In 1896 Steinlen drew The Street for a poster: working women, children, the well-to-do, policemen, everyone on the same pavement. He loved the people at the bottom. The pavement hasn't changed.
nike-la-police.note: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen, The Street, poster for the printer Charles Verneau, 1896.

art.commons: Affiches Charles Verneau. "La Rue " - affiche - Steinlen 96 - btv1b9011731v.jpg
art.caption: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen, The Street, 1896

scene: In the morning the street belongs to those who work. Washerwomen carry their baskets on their hips, a child drags a bundle of firewood, a cat sleeps on a windowsill in the only patch of sun.

Two policemen walk by slowly, capes over their shoulders, looking at everyone as if we owed them something. The washerwomen go quiet as they pass and laugh as soon as their backs are turned. A painter on the corner sketches it all in charcoal: the women, the child, the cat, the policemen.

Later his drawing will cover the walls of Paris, a whole street of people on a single poster. Everyone will recognise themselves in it. That is what a wall is for: so that the people who have no newspaper can still say something.
nike-la-police.approach: Last wall. The same pink, a different anger. I put my camera away. The walk ends here, but the walls go on talking.

start.title: Point Zero, square in front of Notre-Dame
